## Website Designer in Pune: How to Write Page Titles and Meta Descriptions That Get Clicked — What Google Shows, What It Rewrites and a Template for Service Pages

A good title tag for a service page names the service, the place and one reason to choose you, in roughly 50 to 60 characters so that it is unlikely to be cut off, and it matches what the page really says. A good meta description is a two-sentence promise of what the visitor will find, written for a person and not for a ranking formula. Google has no fixed character limit for either; what it does is truncate by display width and, when it thinks your text is a poor description of the page, replace it. So the practical job of a website designer in Pune, and of the business owner briefing one, is to write snippets that are accurate, specific and short enough to survive, then check in Search Console whether they are actually earning clicks.

This guide is written for owners and marketing managers of Pune service businesses — clinics, coaching classes, interior designers, CAs, event firms, repair services, B2B suppliers — whose website already exists and appears in Google but gets fewer clicks than it should. It explains what title tags and meta descriptions do, what Google's own documentation says about them, how to write them for a service website, how to fix the common failures, and how to measure whether a change worked.

### What this guide will and will not promise

Rewriting snippets is one of the cheaper SEO tasks, and it can lift click-through rate when the current text is vague or truncated. It will not move you from page three to page one by itself, and nobody can honestly promise a specific percentage improvement. Published click-through studies vary widely by query type, position and industry, and we have not cited a single average here because none transfers reliably to your pages. Treat anything you read that quotes a precise "CTR lift from better titles" with caution; measure your own pages instead, which this guide shows you how to do.

## What a title tag and a meta description actually are

Both live in the head section of a page's HTML, invisible on the page itself.

- The **title element** (`<title>`) names the page. Browsers show it on the tab, bookmarks use it, and search engines treat it as the main source for the clickable blue headline in results.
- The **meta description** (`<meta name="description" content="...">`) is a short summary. Search engines may show it as the grey text under the headline.

Google's Search Central documentation on title links says that Google generates the title link from several sources, mainly the title element, but also headings, other prominent text and anchor text pointing to the page. Its documentation on snippets says that Google uses the meta description when it describes the page better than text taken from the page itself, and otherwise builds a snippet from the page content. Both documents are listed in the sources at the end. The consequence is important: you write the title and description as a proposal, and Google decides what to display for each query. Your aim is to make your proposal the best available answer so that it is used.

### Titles are a ranking input; descriptions are not

Google's documentation describes the title element as an important signal for understanding what a page is about. The meta description is not a ranking factor; it only influences the snippet, and therefore indirectly clicks. This distinction decides where to spend effort. The title needs the words people search for. The description needs the words that persuade a person who has already seen the headline.

## How long should they be?

There is no official character count. Google's documents say that titles and snippets are truncated when they are too long for the display, and the display is measured in pixels, not characters. A title full of wide letters such as "W" and "M" is cut sooner than one with narrow letters. The numbers below are working guidelines used by practitioners, not rules from Google.

| Element | Working target | Why |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Title | About 50–60 characters | Usually fits on desktop results without an ellipsis; mobile can be a little different |
| Meta description | About 120–155 characters | Long enough for a promise and a call to action; longer text is often trimmed |
| Brand name in title | At the end, short | The service and place should come first because the front of the title is read first |

If your most important words are in the first 40 characters, truncation costs you little even when it happens. That is the habit to build: put the service and the place early, and the nice-to-haves late.

### A note on testing length

Do not trust a plugin's green traffic light alone. Search for your own page after it is re-crawled, look at how it appears on a phone and on a desktop, and see where it breaks. Pixel-width checkers exist, but the actual search result page is the only reliable test, and Search Console's performance report will tell you which query-and-page pairs have low click-through despite a decent position.

## Why Google rewrites your title or description

Many owners discover that the title they carefully wrote does not appear in Google. Google's own documentation lists common reasons for a rewrite, and each one maps to something you can fix.

1. **Half-empty or default titles.** Titles such as "Home", "Untitled" or "Welcome to our website" give no information, so Google uses a heading or other text instead.
2. **Stuffed or repetitive titles.** A title that repeats the same phrase, or lists many cities, looks manipulative and is often replaced.
3. **Same title on many pages.** If dozens of pages share one title, Google cannot distinguish them and substitutes page-specific text.
4. **A mismatch with the page.** If the title promises something the visible page does not deliver, Google leans on the on-page heading.
5. **A very long title.** It may be shortened or replaced.

For descriptions the common causes are: no description at all, a generic site-wide description used on every page, a description that does not mention what the searcher typed, and text copied from a template. In each case Google builds its own snippet from the page. That is not a penalty. It is a signal that your proposal was weaker than the page text.

### Rewrites are not always bad

Sometimes Google's rewrite is better than ours. Look at what it chose. If it pulled your H1, that tells you the H1 is a good description and the title could use it. If it appended your brand name, you may be able to shorten your own brand suffix. Learn from the rewrite instead of fighting it.

## A repeatable method for writing a title

For a Pune service business, a dependable structure is:

**[Service] in [Locality or City] — [Differentiator or proof] | [Brand]**

Each part has a job.

### 1. Lead with the service the visitor searches for

Use the phrase customers use, not the one on your brochure. Someone looking for a dentist searches "dentist in Kothrud", not "advanced oral wellness centre". Keyword research does not have to be elaborate: look at your Search Console queries, the "People also ask" box for the topic, and how your callers describe their problem. Our guide on [mapping keywords to search intent](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-keyword-research-search-intent-mapping-2026) explains how to decide which phrase belongs on which page.

### 2. Add the place only where the page is truly about the place

A page for a business with one clinic in Kothrud can honestly say "Kothrud, Pune". A page that lists "Pune, Pimpri, Chinchwad, Hinjewadi, Baner, Wakad" in the title is a keyword string and is more likely to be rewritten. If you serve several areas, the right fix is to make real service-area pages with unique content, not to cram names into one title. We discuss the line between a useful location page and a thin one in our piece on [service-area pages and doorway pages](/blog/website-designer-pune-service-area-location-pages-doorway-2026).

### 3. Give one honest reason to choose you

This is the differentiator: "same-day estimate", "fixed-price packages", "NABL-accredited lab", "Marathi and English support". It must be true and checkable. Avoid superlatives you cannot prove, such as "best" or "No. 1". Google's guidance on helpful content stresses accuracy and trust, and a visitor who sees "best" in a result has learned to discount it.

### 4. Add the brand last, and keep it short

"| Govindani Infotech" costs about 20 characters. On a page where space is tight, drop the brand and keep the proposition. On the home page, put the brand first.

### Worked examples

These examples are illustrative templates, not real client titles.

| Page | Weak title | Stronger title |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Dental clinic home page | Home – Smile Care | Dentist in Kothrud, Pune — Painless Root Canal & Braces \| Smile Care |
| Interior designer service page | Services | Home Interior Designer in Pune — 2 & 3 BHK Packages \| Studio Name |
| CA firm GST page | GST Services Pune Pune GST Pune CA | GST Registration & Return Filing in Pune — Fixed Monthly Fees \| Firm Name |
| Coaching class | Welcome to our classes | Class 10 CBSE Maths Coaching in Baner, Pune — Small Batches \| Class Name |
| Local repair service | Best AC repair Pune cheap AC service | AC Repair & Service in Pune — Visit Within 24 Hours \| Brand |

Notice that every stronger title contains one thing you could verify by calling the business: a service area, a package, a fee structure, a response time. If the business cannot honour the claim, do not put it in the title.

## A repeatable method for writing a meta description

The description's job is to turn a glance into a click. It has about two sentences.

1. **Say what the page offers, using the searcher's words.** Google bolds matching words in snippets, which draws the eye.
2. **Add one concrete detail.** A price range, a timeline, a location, a document the visitor can download.
3. **End with a soft action.** "Get a quote", "See packages", "Book a visit".

Example for a service page: "Fixed-price website packages for Pune clinics, with appointment booking and Google Business Profile setup. See what is included and request a quote." That is about 150 characters, names the audience, states two features and ends on an action.

### Things to leave out

- Phone numbers and long address strings; they waste space and appear elsewhere in results.
- Unusual symbols and emoji; they add little and may be dropped.
- Claims of "guaranteed results".
- Anything that is not on the page. If the description promises a free checklist, the page must offer it.

## Uniqueness: the problem behind most weak snippets

The most common failure we see on small-business sites is not bad copy, it is no copy. The website platform fills in a default title using the page name and the site name, and every description is empty or identical. If you have 30 pages, you need 30 titles and 30 descriptions, each written for that page.

### How to audit what you have

1. In Google Search Console, open the Pages report and the Performance report. Export the list of pages with their impressions and clicks.
2. Crawl your site with a free or paid crawler (Screaming Frog has a free tier limited by URL count) and export the title and meta description columns. A spreadsheet is enough.
3. Mark duplicates, empties and over-long entries.
4. Prioritise the pages that already have impressions but few clicks. These are the pages where better snippets can help the most, because Google is already showing them.

An honest warning: Search Console shows impressions and clicks per query only for queries it reports, and small sites often have low volume. Do not draw conclusions from a handful of clicks. Wait for a few weeks of data before judging a change.

### Platform-specific notes

- **WordPress:** an SEO plugin gives each page a title and description field. Rank Math, Yoast and similar plugins all work. The risk is a template pattern such as "%%title%% %%sep%% %%sitename%%" applied to every page without review. Check the real output, not just the template.
- **Shopify and WooCommerce:** product and collection pages generate titles from the product name by default. For collection pages, write a title that matches the category search, not only the collection's internal name. Our guide to [collection page SEO content](/blog/ecommerce-website-development-pune-collection-page-seo-content-2026) covers that case.
- **Custom-coded sites:** make sure each route sets its own title and description in the server-rendered HTML, not only after JavaScript runs. A site that sets the title in the browser can show the wrong snippet to crawlers that do not execute scripts. This is a build requirement, not an afterthought, and it is the kind of detail we check when we scope a [custom website build](/services/website-creation).

## Matching the title to the page: the H1 relationship

The title tag and the H1 do not need to be identical, but they should clearly describe the same page. A common pattern is to make the H1 slightly longer and more natural, because the visitor sees it after clicking, and the title shorter and more keyword-led, because the searcher sees it in results. If they contradict each other, Google may display your H1 or other text instead. See our guide on [site structure and internal linking](/blog/web-development-company-pune-internal-linking-breadcrumbs-site-architecture-2026) for how page titles also appear in breadcrumbs.

## Structured data and snippets

Structured data does not set the title or description, but it can change how a result looks. Marking up an article, a business or an event can make a result eligible for richer display where Google supports it, and Google states that markup does not guarantee a rich result. Use it where it is honest, as covered in our guide to [schema markup for business websites](/blog/web-development-company-pune-structured-data-schema-markup-2026). Do not add review markup for reviews you wrote about yourself; Google's guidance treats self-serving review markup as ineligible for star results.

## Measuring whether it worked

You can run a simple, honest before-and-after check without special tools.

1. **Pick up to ten pages** with at least a few hundred impressions in the last 28 days.
2. **Record** for each page the clicks, impressions, average position and CTR from Search Console's Performance report, filtered by page.
3. **Change only the title and description**, nothing else, so that the cause is clear. Request re-indexing for each page with the URL Inspection tool.
4. **Wait four to six weeks**, then compare the same measures for a period of the same length.
5. **Judge cautiously.** If position moved, click-through may have changed for that reason alone. Seasonality, a Google update or a competitor's change can all affect a result. Look for a consistent direction across several pages, not a single dramatic one.

### What a realistic result looks like

Some pages will improve, some will not, and some will worsen. That is normal. Keep what worked, revert what clearly did not, and write down why. After two rounds you will know the style that earns clicks for your own audience, and that knowledge is worth more than a borrowed statistic.

## Common mistakes

1. **One title for the whole site.** Every page needs its own.
2. **Keyword lists.** "Website designer Pune, web design Pune, web developer Pune" reads as spam, and Google may rewrite it.
3. **Brand-first on every page.** The brand is rarely what a new searcher is looking for.
4. **Promising what the page does not contain.** It raises bounce and invites rewrites.
5. **Changing everything at once.** If you cannot tell which change worked, you cannot repeat it.
6. **Forgetting mobile.** Check how the result displays on a phone, where most local searches happen.
7. **Never revisiting.** Prices, offers and locations change; so should the snippet.

## A one-week plan for a small site

- **Day 1:** Export current titles and descriptions. Mark duplicates and empties.
- **Day 2:** List your ten most important pages, those that bring enquiries.
- **Day 3:** Write new titles using the structure above. Have one other person read them for accuracy.
- **Day 4:** Write descriptions. Remove anything the page does not support.
- **Day 5:** Publish the changes and request indexing for the ten pages.
- **Day 6:** Record your baseline numbers from Search Console.
- **Day 7:** Set a calendar reminder for four weeks later to compare.

If you have a content management system that makes this tedious, that is a sign the site's setup deserves attention. Better structure also helps the rest of your search presence, and our guide to a [content refresh and decay audit](/blog/digital-marketing-agency-pune-seo-content-refresh-decay-audit-2026) shows how to decide which older pages are worth revisiting first.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the ideal length for a title tag?
There is no official limit. Google truncates by display width, so a practical target is roughly 50 to 60 characters with the service and place near the front. Check the actual result on mobile and desktop.

### Does the meta description affect my Google ranking?
Not directly. Google's documentation treats the description as a candidate for the snippet, not a ranking signal, but a more persuasive snippet can earn more clicks from the same position.

### Why does Google show a different title from the one I wrote?
Google builds title links from several sources and may replace a title that is empty, stuffed with keywords, identical across many pages or inconsistent with the page content. Fix the cause rather than rewriting repeatedly.

### Should I include my city in every title?
Only where the page is truly about that city or area. Repeating several localities in one title tends to look like keyword stuffing; create genuine location pages instead.

### How long before new titles and descriptions show in Google?
It depends on how often Google crawls the page. Requesting indexing in Search Console can speed it up, but allow several weeks before judging the result.

## Where to Start

Choose the five pages that bring you the most enquiries. Write a specific title and description for each, publish, and write down today's click-through rate. Look again in a month. If your site's platform makes per-page control difficult, or if titles are set by JavaScript that crawlers may not read, talk to your developer about fixing the foundation first.
